english.html: brothers and certain kinsfolk of the said Tilh, so that the two men might be exhibited to them severally and together, and they might choose from them the one whom they recognised to be truly Martin Guerre. All the said witnesses come, save the brothers of the said du Tilh, who, by multiplication of penalties, letters and commands, could not be forced to come and depose against their brother.

These persons certainly deserved some excuse for not being willing to depose against their own brother; to which also the law has not willed to constrain them <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, even when it is a matter of a thing so weighty as a capital crime <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. And in truth it would be a thing too near to inhumanity to force a man to ruin and destroy his bones, his blood and his own flesh <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup> — which no one, says the Apostle, ever held in hatred <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>, he esteeming him who has no care for his own to be worse than an infidel <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>. Which has moved our Interpreters to teach that he who has promised to lend the Prince some castle or fortress, generally against all comers, is nevertheless not bound to lend it against himself <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>, nor against his father, mother, children, brothers and other near kinsfolk, who by nature are scarcely less dear to him than himself <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>.

Si testes), at § Lege Iulia and at the penultimate paragraph (§ pe. = penultimo)
notes.original: l. lege Iulia. D. de teſti. c ſi teſtes. P. lege Iulia, & P. pe. iiij. q. iij.
notes.gloss: Gratian's long canon on witnesses incorporates the Digest text; the print's P. is its sort for §.

notes.citation: Code 9.1 (Qui accusare non possunt), l. Si magnum and l. Si sororem (fragment numbers not verified)
notes.original: l. ſi magnũ. l. ſi ſororem. C. qui acq. non poſ.
notes.gloss: Constitutions on who may not accuse; cited for the rule that kin are not compelled to proceed against kin even in capital matters. The print's acq. is for accusare.

notes.citation: Code 5.62 (De excusationibus et temporibus earum, the title on excuses from guardianship), l. Humanitatis (fragment number not verified)
notes.original: l. humanitatis. C. de excuſ. tuto.
notes.gloss: A law that begins by appealing to humanity (humanitatis ratio); cited for the principle that the law does not demand what is inhuman.
Nemo enim umquam carnem suam odio habuit: no man ever hated his own flesh.

notes.original: La j. de Timoth. c. v.
notes.gloss: He that has no care for his own, and especially for those of his house, has denied the faith and is worse than an infidel.

notes.citation: The Gloss on c. Petitio, Decretals X 2.24 (De iureiurando) (chapter number not verified; the same chapter is cited at annot-046 {b}); Bartolus (Barto) on Digest 1.9.1 (De senatoribus, l. 1, Ulpian)
notes.original: Gloſe au c. petitio, de iureiu Barto in la l. j. D. de ſenator.
notes.gloss: The doctors' limitation of a general promise or oath: it does not bind against oneself.

notes.citation: Baldus (Balde) on Code 6.42 (De fideicommissis), l. Cum acutissimi (fragment number not verified); the Masters (the doctors) on Digest 12.6.38 (De condictione indebiti, l. Frater a fratre, Africanus)
notes.original: Balde en la l. cũ accutiſsimi C. de fidei com. Les maiſtres en la l. frater à fratre. D. de cõd. Indebiti.
notes.gloss: Both cited for the extension of "oneself" to one's nearest kin, whom nature makes as dear as oneself; Frater a fratre treats brothers under one patria potestas.

english.html: The eldest sister arrives first, who, after having contemplated the newcomer a little while, recognises him for her brother, and weeping goes to embrace him.
